summary: Eliminating an unresolved diffusion field from a coupled parabolic system produces an operator-valued memory term and a contribution from the hidden initial state. We study whether a reduced prediction of the retained field meets a prescribed tolerance. For known hidden initial data, the discarded response, damped by diffusion and transmitted through the coupling, gives an upper error bound; an auxiliary diffusion problem supplies a lower bound. Rigorous discretisation bounds then yield tests that accept, reject or remain undecided. If the discarded initial state is known only through a norm bound, the minimum worst-case error equals that bound multiplied by the time-uniform gain from the missing state to the retained trajectory. Our main result encloses this infinite-dimensional gain using a finite spectral Galerkin evolution, its residual in the full equations and an explicit diffusion tail. The enclosure converges without compactness or smallness of the coupling. Strict comparisons of the optimal radius with a tolerance have finite certificates if all endpoint quantities admit arbitrarily accurate rigorous enclosures. Multiplication-coupling examples with infinitely many dynamically coupled modes illustrate both settings, including explicit finite-element error budgets.

title: Computational performance versus numerical accuracy in the acoustic terms of weakly-compressible SPH
summary: Accurate computation of the acoustic terms in weakly-compressible SPH, including the equation of state, its inverse, and the evaluation of the local speed of sound, is essential to ensure energy conservation, robust solid boundary conditions, and correct open boundary behavior. In the classic Cole's equation of state, using values of the polytropic constant $γ\ne 1$ can lead to significant precision loss, particularly when computations are performed in single precision, as is common in GPU implementations. We extend here our previous results on the optimal choice of state variable by introducing a new higher-precision form for all three acoustic terms, denoted \texttt{explog}, and assess its numerical accuracy and computational performance across a variety of devices and test cases. We find that the new form evaluates the acoustic terms with a maximum ULP of~2 for arguments less than $0.125$, and has higher errors in less than 1\% of the arguments larger than the threshold. Combined with a rewritten expression of the pressure at solid boundary particles in the ``dummy'' model, it provides consistently more accurate results, maintaining deviations from the reference pressure profile to below 2\%, even in presence of a rough bottom terrain. Computationally, the new formulation is also faster than the naive one on GPU, and only marginally slower on CPU.

title: Adaptive accuracy-driven splitting in Ozaki matrix multiplication and application to block LU factorization
summary: The Ozaki scheme for matrix multiplication computes an accurate matrix product by splitting the input matrices and evaluating a sequence of low-precision matrix products. Its accuracy and computational cost depend strongly on the number of splits. We develop accuracy-driven criteria for selecting this number in both Ozaki matrix multiplication and in block LU factorization using Ozaki trailing updates. For matrix multiplication, we derive normwise and componentwise criteria that determine how many split products are required to achieve a given accuracy requirement. For block LU, we present a fixed normwise strategy with essentially no selection cost, an LU-aware adaptive normwise strategy that can reduce the number of splits in subsequent trailing updates, and a componentwise strategy that uses information accumulated from preceding updates to guide the later selections. In the componentwise strategy, when the required number of splits exceeds a prescribed maximum, the corresponding update is instead carried out using ordinary matrix multiplication. We also provide rigorous backward error bounds for these approaches. Numerical experiments show that the adaptive normwise strategy can reduce the number of splits while preserving normwise accuracy, whereas the componentwise strategy can provide smaller componentwise backward errors when stronger local accuracy is needed.

title: Multi-GPU Acceleration of Interface Problems in FEniCS, with Application to Cardiac Modeling
summary: GPU acceleration of finite element assembly is well established for standard formulations, but mixed-dimensional problems, in which volumetric subdomains are coupled via lower-dimensional interfaces, remain unsupported in automated frameworks such as FEniCS. We extend cuDOLFINx, a GPU-enabled extension of the DOLFINx finite element framework, to assemble such interface problems on GPUs while preserving the high-level FEniCS programming model. Combined with GPU-resident Krylov solvers and algebraic multigrid preconditioning, this enables end-to-end GPU execution of the EMI (Extracellular--Membrane--Intracellular) model, an elliptic interface problem from cardiac modeling in which many intracellular subdomains are coupled through membranes. We compare the GPU implementation against a CPU-based one through strong and weak scaling experiments on regular and realistic 3D cardiac geometries with up to 8000 cells and 22 million degrees of freedom. In terms of assembly, a single GH200 node is roughly equivalent to two 144-core CPU nodes in strong scaling, and to two to three nodes in weak scaling, depending on geometry. For the linear solver, performance depends on geometry, preconditioning, and problem scale. On the regular geometry, GPU advantages emerge mainly at larger problem sizes and node counts. On the realistic geometry, with the same algebraic multigrid preconditioner for both architectures, the GPU is faster at all tested scales. The implementation is available as open-source software and applies to other problems with interface coupling.

title: Kernelized Stable Fluids for simulating physically accurate solutions
summary: The Stable Fluids algorithm is a fractional step method for solving the incompressible Navier-Stokes (NS) equations in an unconditionally stable way. It was initially developed for visual effects and allows real-time simulations because of its low computational complexity. The method solves the advection step by using the method of characteristics which is implemented via linear interpolation. This results in excessive diffusion of vorticity and is one of the main reasons for the physical inaccuracy of the algorithm. We propose Kernelized Stable Fluids with Sparse Cholesky Preconditioning (KSF-Chol) in order to address this shortcoming and make the algorithm thereby suitable for engineering problems and scientific computing. The algorithm is modified by replacing the linear interpolation approach with kernel interpolation in the advection step. We accelerate the computationally expensive kernel interpolation by using sparse Cholesky preconditioning and a near-/far-field approach and optimize both methods for computations on a uniform Cartesian grid. KSF-Chol achieves per time step a near-linear computational complexity of $\mathcal{O}(N\log^d(N/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{chol}}))$ in space and time. We test KSF-Chol against reference solvers and numerical reference data on multiple 2D and 3D benchmarks and demonstrate a significantly reduced numerical diffusion as well as a competitive accuracy concerning the computation of relevant flow quantities.

title: Quadrature Perturbations and High-Order Time Discretization for Prescribed-Feature Evolutionary GTransNet Galerkin Systems
summary: In this paper we study quadrature perturbations and high-order time discretization for a prescribed-feature evolutionary generalized transferable neural network (Evo-GTransNet) Galerkin method for linear self-adjoint parabolic equations. Assembly quadrature, together with truncated singular value decomposition, is used to select a numerically resolved trial space and obtain coordinates with an identity mass matrix. Since this normalization depends on the assembly quadrature, the retained functions are also evaluated using a separate comparison quadrature, which is finer in the numerical experiments. For the two resulting semidiscrete systems, we derive an exact equation for the difference between their trajectories and an energy estimate that separates errors arising from the effective operator, load vector, and initial projection. The estimate is conditional on the trial space selected by the assembly quadrature. The retained rank, discarded mass, cross mass, and principal angles are used to assess this selection step. Refining the comparison quadrature yields stable retained spaces for the reported configurations, whereas deliberate underintegration leads to much larger perturbations. On the fixed retained systems, the temporal convergence of implicit midpoint, BDF, Radau IIA, and Gauss--Legendre methods is consistent with their classical orders over the resolved refinement ranges. The experiments distinguish the retained-coordinate error from the total solution error; the latter is measured against the PDE solution in the $L^2$ norm, with the error integrals evaluated by sufficiently fine quadrature. They also illustrate the importance of suitable starting values for BDF3 and show how the performance of IMEX-BDF schemes depends on the operator splitting and time step size.

title: Scalable Fully Implicit Runge-Kutta Solvers for Time-Dependent Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
comment: 26 pages, 10 tables, and 7 figures, submitted for publication in the SIAM journal on scientific computing (SISC) special section, 41st Colorado Conference Iterative and Multigrid Methods 2026
summary: We consider the efficient numerical solution of time-dependent Rayleigh-Bénard convection governed by the incompressible Boussinesq equations. The coupled velocity-pressure-temperature system presents significant computational challenges arising from incompressibility, buoyancy coupling, convection, and the simultaneous resolution of multiple physical time scales. We present a systematic study of fully implicit Runge-Kutta methods for time-dependent Rayleigh-Bénard convection, together with scalable finite element solvers for the resulting stage-coupled systems. We employ high-order, L-stable Radau IIA methods for temporal integration and investigate Taylor-Hood and Alfeld-Sorokina finite elements in two dimensions, along with Taylor-Hood and enriched macroelement discretizations in three dimensions. The macroelement approaches offer strong local inf-sup stability and patch structures well suited to Vanka-type relaxation. In two dimensions, monolithic multigrid achieves nearly stage-independent outer Krylov iteration counts and maintains robust convergence under mesh refinement. On the same mesh with incremental pressure correction, selected Radau configurations reduce elapsed solve time by 18-32% and yield smaller sampled transient differences relative to a numerical reference solution. Three-dimensional experiments demonstrate favorable parallel scalability with Taylor-Hood elements and substantially improved discrete mass conservation with the enriched macroelement discretization. These results identify regimes in which coupled multistage fully implicit integration is computationally competitive when equipped with appropriate multigrid preconditioners.

title: Optimal bounds for design curves on the torus
summary:
A closed rectifiable curve on the torus $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ is a $t$-design curve if normalized arclength integration is exact for trigonometric polynomials $e^{2πi \langle m,x\rangle}$ with frequencies $m\in\mathbb Z^d$ satisfying $\|m\|_\infty\le t$. For the arclength $L$ of such curves, we establish the sharp lower bound \begin{equation}\label{eq:abs} L\geq \Big(\frac{(t+1)^{2d}-1}{t(t+2)}\Big)^{1/2}. \end{equation} Equality is attained by the family of Korobov curves described in \cite{Kunis,Lindblad}.
  For even $t$, we also derive an explicit lower bound on the length of total-degree $t$-design curves, defined by the frequency condition $\|m\|_1\leq t$. This bound is sharp for $t=2$ in every dimension and for every even $t$ in dimension two.
  We determine the minimum length of hyperbolic cross $t^2$-design curves in dimension two. For $d\geq3$, we establish lower bounds of optimal order for the length of hyperbolic cross $t^d$-design curves.
  Finally, we obtain lower bounds of optimal order for the length of $t$-design curves associated with sparse frequency sets.

title: First- and second-order constrained optimisation for inverse homogenisation of unidirectionally varying microstructure
summary: This paper is concerned with inverse homogenisation problems that aim to identify microstructure features of a body from macroscopic measurements. The unknown microstructure is assumed to vary macroscopically in one spatial direction and affects the effective tensor in an elliptic partial differential equation that governs the behaviour of the body on the macroscale. We establish the well-posedness of the PDE-constrained minimisation problems that model the task of identifying the microstructure, derive first-order necessary optimality conditions, and prove the convergence of a gradient-projection algorithm for the studied problem class in an infinite-dimensional setting. We moreover demonstrate that recently obtained results on generalised differentiability properties of solution maps of bilateral obstacle problems make it possible to set up and analyse a novel semismooth Newton method in the considered situation. The functional analytic setting that we use for our investigation is chosen such that it covers various elliptic PDEs simultaneously (classical second-order equations, bi-Laplace problems, linear elasticity, etc.) and explicitly exploits the problem structure to obtain global convergence guarantees for the studied solution algorithms in terms of the Lipschitz constants of the involved operators. Our analysis is accompanied by numerical experiments which show that the new semismooth Newton approach requires far less expensive projection evaluations than the gradient-descent method and, thus, offers a significant speedup.

title: Rate optimality of AFEM with maximum marking
summary: For Poisson's equation, we prove optimal algebraic convergence rates for adaptive conforming finite element methods driven by standard maximum marking in arbitrary space dimension, for every marking parameter in $(0,1]$. Previously, instance optimality of a modified maximum marking was proved in [L. Diening, C. Kreuzer, and R. Stevenson, Instance optimality of the adaptive maximum strategy, Found. Comput. Math., 16 (2016), pp. 33--68]. The basic ingredients of our anlaysis consists of discrete reliability, discrete efficiency, overlay and closure estimates of local mesh refinement. The discrete efficiency requires a facet-interior node property of simplicial mesh refinement. The novel part of the optimality analysis is an elementary integral-sum argument that converts energy decrease into a cumulative cardinality bound of marked elements, yielding rate optimality without a contraction argument.

title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 3D
summary: Overlapping Schwarz methods are among the most successful domain decomposition preconditioners for large-scale finite element simulations. In this work, the Generalized Dryja-Smith-Widlund (GDSW), GDSW$^*$, and Reduced GDSW (RGDSW) coarse spaces are studied for three-dimensional high-order finite element method (FEM) and virtual element method (VEM) for the Poisson equation and the equations of linear elasticity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of GDSW-type coarse spaces for polynomial degrees $k\ge 3$ in three dimensions, for either discretization. In 3D VEM, the face degrees of freedom (DOFs) are moments instead of point values. The kernel of the differential operator, which defines the interface values of the GDSW coarse basis functions, must be represented through these moments. The construction is therefore no longer purely algebraic and, without this correction, the coarse level loses its effect for $k\ge 3$. FEM and VEM are tested on hexahedral meshes, and VEM is additionally tested on polyhedral ones. Polynomial degrees up to $k=5$ and runs on up to $4\,096$ subdomains and parallel cores are included in the numerical study. Numerical experiments show scalable iteration counts for all coarse space variants for the Poisson problem, illustrating the expected trade-off between the coarse space size and robustness. Further experiments for linear elasticity confirms that the moment-based construction extends naturally from the scalar to the vector-valued problem.

title: Lattice Green's functions for Poisson problems with two unbounded and one periodic direction
summary: Fourier-based Poisson solvers treat periodic directions spectrally and unbounded ones by the Hockney--Eastwood convolution with a free-space kernel. With two unbounded and one periodic direction, the setting of vortex tubes, wakes and jets, the kernel used so far by these solvers combines the two-dimensional kernel on the zero periodic mode with the symbol of the operator sampled on the doubled grid on every other mode. We show that the second ingredient is not exact: the error is the field of the periodic images of the source and independent of the mesh size. While the period $L_z$ is not much longer than the unbounded extent $L_x$, it is of order $\exp(-2πd/L_z)$, with $d$ the distance to the nearest image; beyond, it grows like $(L_z/L_x)^2$. The error is thus small on cubic domains, but larger than the solution itself on elongated ones. We remove the approximation by extending the integral representation of the exact second-order kernel of Hou and Colonius: the screened kernel of each mode is evaluated in closed form along one unbounded direction and by Gauss--Legendre quadrature along the other, for the high-order dimension-split and Mehrstellen stencils, at a one-off cost of about one solve. The kernels, implemented in the open-source library \flups{}, are verified by comparison with independent quadratures, by a padding test sensitive to the boundary condition enforced, and by convergence at the order of each stencil on an axially modulated tube source, on domains up to $64$ times longer than wide and up to $2.7\times10^{11}$ unknowns.

title: Symbol-based residual certification of reduced and neural surrogates for tempered-fractional CGMY pricing
summary: We certify reduced and neural approximations of European-put price trajectories under the Carr--Geman--Madan--Yor model by residual bounds for the spline Galerkin discretisation of the tempered-fractional pricing equation. The Galerkin matrices are Toeplitz sections of an explicit periodised Fourier symbol; summing the alias series to a stated tail makes the assembled system exact to $10^{-8}$. A Lévy--Khintchine argument gives the parameter-explicit bound $λ_{\min}(S_I)\ge r\,m_{\min}$ for the symmetric part, valid for $Y\in(0,2)\setminus\{1\}$, replacing numerical spectral estimates. A banded comparison norm built from the mass and stiffness symbols yields a rigorous certificate at $O(N)$ cost with explicit effectivity, and empirical interpolation of the symbol makes the operator affine in about 36 terms with a rigorous error transfer, so a reduced model is certified at a cost independent of $N$; a three-stage rule escalates to the full-order bounds only when needed. At the resolution that prices the whole parameter box to one cent ($N=1024$), the full-order certificate costs 6% of a direct solve, and the certified POD--Galerkin model of rank 80 costs 3% of it and settles 99.8% of $10^4$ queries without touching the full space. No false accept occurs on any query with a reference solution (150 inside the parameter box, 264 outside), and outside the box the certificate accepts 193 of the 210 queries on which the reduced model is still within one cent. The neural reduced models trained here miss the one-cent tolerance by a factor of at least 46; the certificate detects this at every query in a few milliseconds and explains it as a trade-off between temporal smoothness and coefficient accuracy. A residual certificate for the American put is proved as an outlook.

title: An Active Flux Method for Maxwell's equations
summary: We present a novel Active Flux method and a divergence-free method using exact evolution operators for solving Maxwell's equations in three space dimensions on Cartesian grids. The proposed methods are fully discrete, third-order accurate and rely on a truly multidimensional evolution operator based on Kirchhoff's formula for the electromagnetic wave equation. The first method is a classical Active Flux method with globally continuous reconstruction while the second method is an adaptation of the Active Flux method to a locally divergence-free reconstruction by Balsara. The applied reconstruction is built from facial degrees of freedom and is no longer globally continuous. The classical method keeps the divergence error bounded. The divergence-free method with face averages initialized by a potential keeps the constraints at round-off. We compare the accuracy of both methods for smooth and discontinuous test problems.

title: Structured Neural Network Models for Anisotropic Magnetic Constitutive Laws
summary: High-performance electrical steel used for iron cores of power transformers and generators exhibits complex material behavior. While modeling and simulation of isotropic nonlinear response is well understood, the incorporation of magnetic anisotropy remains challenging. This work proposes to utilize a structured neural network architecture to systematically describe the anisotropic nonlinear anhysteretic magnetic material response of electrical steel sheets. By constructing a convex and smooth co-energy density with dedicated behavior at infinity, we can ensure thermodynamic consistency and correct physical behavior and further guarantee basic mathematical properties which provide well-posedness of corresponding magnetic field problems and efficient numerical solvers. Numerical tests demonstrate the capability of the proposed method to describe strongly anisotropic behavior as well as its robust convergence in finite-element simulations.

title: High-order in-cell discontinuous reconstruction path-conservative methods for conservative systems in primitive variables
summary: We present a path-conservative methodology for the numerical approximation of conservative systems formulated exclusively in primitive variables, the most physically relevant set of variables. The approach is designed to preserve the correct weak solution while avoiding the spurious oscillations near contact discontinuities that may arise in conservative formulations. Nonconservative products are treated through the selection of a suitable family of paths combined with an in-cell discontinuous reconstruction strategy, which is locally activated near shocks. To choose the path we introduce a compatibility condition between the Rankine-Hugoniot conditions of the non-conservative form, with the exact ones, assumed to be known. In smooth regions and across contact discontinuities, a standard path-conservative scheme is employed. The method is further extended to achieve high-order accuracy. Numerical results for the Euler multimaterial and shear interface model demonstrates correct shock-capturing property, suppression of spurious oscillations due to contact discontinuities, and convergence without using hybrid formulations.

title: High-order guaranteed lower bounds for the Schrödinger eigenvalue problem
summary: We compute unconditional guaranteed lower eigenvalue bounds for Schrödinger operators using a modified hybrid high-order method with built-in correction for the potential defect. The method assumes exact numerical integration and allows possibly unbounded potentials in $L^p$ for $p>n/2$ and $p\geq2$ on general polyhedral domains. We prove that the high-order correction preserves optimal a priori convergence orders, and derive reliable and efficient a posteriori error estimators. Numerical experiments provide striking evidence of optimal high-order convergence rates of the adaptive algorithm.

title: Multi-Trajectory Parallel-in-Iteration Optimization
summary: Previously, we developed a ``parallel-in-iteration'' optimization framework that uses multigrid reduction-in-time (MGRIT) to parallelize slowly converging optimization methods, such as gradient descent. Unlike time-dependent evolution problems, optimization requires only a final point with a sufficiently small gradient, rather than an accurate approximation of the entire trajectory of iterates. This motivates a different use of MGRIT: instead of repeatedly improving the approximation of a single long trajectory, we introduce restarted MGRIT (R-MGRIT), which performs one MGRIT iteration on a trajectory, takes the approximate final point as a new initial guess, and repeats the process on a new trajectory. Each restart thus defines a new all-at-once system, allowing progress toward the solution without accurately approximating the preceding trajectory. Moreover, we find that these trajectories can be shortened without increasing the number of restarts needed for convergence. We provide theoretical results comparing MGRIT and R-MGRIT for linear problems and demonstrate the convergence behavior of the shortened trajectories numerically for both linear and nonlinear problems. Shortening the trajectories increases the estimated parallel speedup while reducing the number of processors required.
